The whitetip reef shark Triaenodon obesus is a relatively small-bodied carcharhinid that inhabits shallow coral reef environments across the Indo-Pacific region. Neonates emerge from their mothers at a total length of approximately 60 cm [Lb = approximately 60 cm], a size that reflects the constraints of aplacental viviparous reproduction in this species. Early life stages are characterised by rapid growth during the first few years following parturition, as young individuals must quickly attain a size that reduces predation risk from larger piscivorous fishes and conspecifics. Field studies conducted in the waters surrounding the Hawaiian Archipelago have provided valuable insight into the reproductive biology of this species, though many aspects of its early ontogeny remain poorly resolved due to the logistical difficulties of tracking individuals through the cryptic juvenile phase. The gestation period is relatively protracted for a carcharhinid of this size.

Reproductive activity in Triaenodon obesus is tightly linked to warm-water conditions, with key life-history milestones having been documented primarily at a stable ambient temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C] within the species core habitat range. Under these thermal conditions, the gestation period lasts approximately 10 months, with pups being born after a developmental interval of roughly 305 days [ab = roughly 305 days] following the initial insemination event at a temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]. This extended intrauterine development is consistent with the aplacental viviparous mode observed in many reef-associated carcharhinids, wherein embryos develop within the maternal reproductive tract supported solely by yolk reserves until the moment of parturition. The relatively large size at birth, measured as 60 cm [Lb = 60 cm], suggests that the energetic investment per offspring is considerable, even though litter sizes are modest. The reproductive cycle appears to be synchronised with seasonal fluctuations in water temperature and prey availability, ensuring that neonates are born during periods of maximum foraging opportunity.

Sexual maturation in both male and female whitetip reef sharks occurs over a comparable size range, though subtle differences have been detected across different populations. Males typically attain puberty when they reach a total length of approximately 114 cm [Lp = approximately 114 cm] at a mean water temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], with some individual variation reported between 112 and 116 cm. Females, by contrast, tend to mature at a slightly larger body size, with puberty occurring around 118 cm [Lp = around 118 cm] based on surveys conducted at several Pacific reef sites. This pattern of delayed maturation in females is widespread among elasmobranchs and is generally attributed to the greater somatic investment required to support gestation and parturition. The onset of gonadal activity in both sexes is accompanied by changes in the morphology of the claspers in males and by the development of distinct ovarian follicles in females, signalling the transition from the immature juvenile stage to a reproductively viable adult condition.

The reproductive output of Triaenodon obesus is characterised by modest fecundity and a relatively slow turnover rate, typical of many reef-associated elasmobranchs with conservative life-history strategies. Gravid females typically give birth to between 1 and 4 pups per litter [N_R_i = between 1 and 4 pups per litter], and each female produces approximately 1.5 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 litters per year], a pattern that limits the species intrinsic rate of increase but contributes to the stability of adult population densities. These reproductive parameters were recorded in populations inhabiting waters with a mean annual temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], indicating that even under favourable thermal regimes, this species cannot sustain rapid population turnover. The slow reproductive rate renders the whitetip reef shark particularly vulnerable to overfishing pressure, as population recovery following exploitation is a protracted process spanning multiple decades. Comparisons with other carcharhinid species of similar body size highlight the relatively conservative fecundity of Triaenodon obesus.

Tag-recapture studies and vertebral band-pair analysis conducted at a mean water temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C] have estimated the maximum recorded longevity of Triaenodon obesus at approximately 19 years [am = approximately 19 years]. This lifespan is consistent with the values documented for several other reef-dwelling carcharhinids and reflects the species slow-paced life-history syndrome, characterised by delayed maturity, low reproductive output, and prolonged somatic maintenance. Females can ultimately attain a total length of up to 213 cm [Li = up to 213 cm], though individuals of this size are rarely encountered in contemporary field surveys, likely due to the cumulative effects of fishing mortality on the largest age classes. The conservative reproductive strategy of this species—characterised by small litters and a multi-year breeding interval—renders it intrinsically vulnerable to exploitation, as population recovery following even moderate fishing pressure may require several decades.
